```{=html}
<link rel="stylesheet" href="assets/site.css">
<div class="lp">

<!-- ============ HERO ============ -->
<section class="hero">
  <div class="wrap">
    <div class="eyebrow">A statistics experiment · Central Limit Theorem</div>
    <h1>How fast does<br><span class="bell">normal</span> happen?</h1>
    <p class="lead">
      Statistics classes teach a rule of thumb: once you average <b>30 or more</b> observations,
      the average follows a bell curve. That bell curve is what makes margins of error and
      confidence intervals work. I put the rule to the test with millions of simulated studies,
      on textbook distributions and on real data.
    </p>
    <div class="ctas">
      <a class="btn primary" href="simulator.html">Try the simulator →</a>
      <a class="btn ghost" href="report.html">Read the findings</a>
    </div>
    <div class="facts">
      <div class="fact"><div class="num">10</div><div class="lbl">populations: 5 textbook, 5 real datasets</div></div>
      <div class="fact"><div class="num">100,000</div><div class="lbl">simulated studies for every sample size</div></div>
      <div class="fact"><div class="num">1</div><div class="lbl">rule of thumb under the microscope: n = 30</div></div>
    </div>
  </div>
</section>

<!-- ============ THE IDEA ============ -->
<section class="band">
  <div class="wrap">
    <div class="eyebrow">The idea in three pictures</div>
    <h2 class="lp-h2">Averages forget where they came from</h2>
    <p class="lead">
      Take any population, even a lopsided one. Pick a few values at random and average them.
      Repeat that thousands of times. The averages pile up into a bell curve. That is the
      Central Limit Theorem. The only question is <b>how many values</b> each average needs.
    </p>
    <div class="steps">
      <div class="card">
        <div class="step-num">1</div>
        <h3>Start with a lopsided population</h3>
        <svg class="mini" id="mini-pop" viewBox="0 0 320 150" role="img" aria-label="Histogram of waiting times: most are short, a few are long"></svg>
        <p>Waiting times: most waits are short, a few are very long.</p>
      </div>
      <div class="card">
        <div class="step-num">2</div>
        <h3>Average 5 at a time</h3>
        <svg class="mini" id="mini-n5" viewBox="0 0 320 150" role="img" aria-label="Averages of 5 waiting times compared with a bell curve"></svg>
        <p>Averages of 5 are still lopsided. The red bell curve does not fit yet.</p>
      </div>
      <div class="card">
        <div class="step-num">3</div>
        <h3>Average 71 at a time</h3>
        <svg class="mini" id="mini-n71" viewBox="0 0 320 150" role="img" aria-label="Averages of 71 waiting times matching a bell curve"></svg>
        <p>Averages of 71 match the bell curve. For this population, 30 was not enough.</p>
      </div>
    </div>
  </div>
</section>

<!-- ============ WHY IT MATTERS ============ -->
<section>
  <div class="wrap poll">
    <div>
      <div class="eyebrow">Why anyone should care</div>
      <div class="big-stat">52% <small>± 3.1%</small></div>
    </div>
    <div>
      <h2 class="lp-h2">Every margin of error relies on this theorem</h2>
      <p>
        A pollster asks 1,000 people one question and reports “52%, plus or minus 3.1 points.”
        They never repeat the poll; the bell curve tells them how far off a single poll could be.
        The same logic is behind drug trials, A/B tests on websites, and quality control in factories.
      </p>
      <p>
        <b>If the averages have not become a bell curve yet, those margins of error are wrong</b>,
        and nobody notices, because in real life you only see one sample.
      </p>
    </div>
  </div>
</section>

<!-- ============ THE ANSWER ============ -->
<section class="band" id="answer">
  <div class="wrap">
    <div class="eyebrow">The answer</div>
    <h2 class="lp-h2">So, is 30 enough?</h2>
    <p class="verdict">
      <span class="g">Sometimes 30 is more than enough.</span>
      <span class="o">Often it is not nearly enough.</span>
      <span class="r">And sometimes no number is enough.</span>
    </p>
    <div class="chart-card">
      <div class="legend">
        <span><i style="background:var(--pass)"></i>30 is enough</span>
        <span><i style="background:var(--warn)"></i>needs more than 30</span>
        <span><i style="background:var(--fail)"></i>never becomes normal</span>
        <span>◆ textbook &nbsp; ● real data</span>
      </div>
      <svg id="answer-chart" viewBox="0 0 1000 520" role="img" aria-label="Sample size needed for each population, compared with 30"></svg>
      <p class="note">Smallest sample size at which the averages pass all four of my “normal enough” checks,
        and keep passing for every larger size tested. Log scale. Hover over a dot for details.</p>
    </div>
  </div>
</section>

<!-- ============ WHAT DECIDES IT ============ -->
<section>
  <div class="wrap">
    <div class="eyebrow">What decides the answer</div>
    <h2 class="lp-h2">Three things slow the bell curve down</h2>
    <div class="factors">
      <div class="card factor">
        <div class="icon">↗</div>
        <h3>Lopsidedness</h3>
        <p>The longer one tail, the more values each average needs. One simple formula predicted the
          answer for most populations, textbook and real:</p>
        <div class="formula">n ≈ (skewness ÷ 0.25)²</div>
      </div>
      <div class="card factor">
        <div class="icon">▥</div>
        <h3>Lumpiness</h3>
        <p>Counts like 0, 1, 2 move in steps. Even when they are not very lopsided, the steps keep the
          shape rough for longer. Rare-event counts needed <b><span data-n="binomial"></span></b> values,
          more than the waiting times.</p>
      </div>
      <div class="card factor">
        <div class="icon">⚡</div>
        <h3>Extreme values</h3>
        <p>If giant values are common enough, averaging never tames them. For the Cauchy distribution
          no sample size works: averaging 5,000 values is no better than looking at one.</p>
      </div>
    </div>
  </div>
</section>

<!-- ============ REAL LIFE ============ -->
<section class="band">
  <div class="wrap">
    <div class="eyebrow">Real data, real consequences</div>
    <h2 class="lp-h2">What this means for actual data</h2>
    <p class="lead">To trust an ordinary 95% interval for the average of…</p>
    <div class="real">
      <div class="card"><div class="what">…flight delays at NYC airports</div>
        <div class="n bad"><span data-n="flights"></span> flights</div>
        <p>Most flights are on time, but a few are hours late. With 30 flights the “95%” interval misses
          on the high side <span data-tail="flights"></span> of the time instead of 2.5%.</p></div>
      <div class="card"><div class="what">…diamond prices</div>
        <div class="n bad"><span data-n="diamonds"></span> diamonds</div>
        <p>A few very expensive stones stretch the price distribution, so 30 diamonds are not quite enough.</p></div>
      <div class="card"><div class="what">…county populations in the US Midwest</div>
        <div class="n bad"><span data-n="counties"></span> counties</div>
        <p>A handful of giant counties (Chicago’s Cook County has 5 million people; the typical county has
          35,000) make the average jump around. That is more than five times the 437 counties these five states actually have.</p></div>
      <div class="card"><div class="what">…waiting times at Old Faithful geyser</div>
        <div class="n ok"><span data-n="faithful"></span> eruptions</div>
        <p>The waits come in two humps, short and long, but are nearly symmetric. Here the rule of 30 is
          more than enough.</p></div>
    </div>
  </div>
</section>

<!-- ============ TRY IT ============ -->
<section>
  <div class="wrap">
    <div class="cta-band">
      <div>
        <h2 class="lp-h2">See it happen yourself</h2>
        <p>Pick a population (a textbook one or real data), choose a sample size, and watch
          thousands of averages pile up into a bell curve, or refuse to.</p>
      </div>
      <a class="btn" href="simulator.html">Open the simulator →</a>
    </div>
  </div>
</section>

<!-- ============ HOW JUDGED ============ -->
<section class="band">
  <div class="wrap">
    <div class="eyebrow">How I judged “normal enough”</div>
    <h2 class="lp-h2">Four checks, one standard for everyone</h2>
    <p class="lead">There is no official cutoff, so I defined one and applied it to every population.
      The averages count as normal enough only when all four checks pass.</p>
    <div class="checks">
      <div class="card"><h3>Not lopsided</h3><p>Skewness between −0.25 and 0.25.</p></div>
      <div class="card"><h3>No excess extremes</h3><p>Excess kurtosis between −0.5 and 0.5.</p></div>
      <div class="card"><h3>Straight Q-Q plot</h3><p>Correlation of at least 0.998 with a perfect bell curve.</p></div>
      <div class="card"><h3>Honest 95% intervals</h3><p>On each side, 1.75%–3.25% of averages fall outside (the ideal is 2.5%).</p></div>
    </div>
    <p class="note" style="margin-top:18px">Each threshold was calibrated by simulation:
      <a href="methods.html">see how and why</a>. I also report every result under a stricter and a more lenient standard.</p>
  </div>
</section>
```
